label: All forest-structure positive/minimal/harm comparisons
quote:
Forest Structure.
The effects of interventions aimed exclu-
sively at altering ground conditions to improve forest structure
were highly variable. In a few cases, treatments had negative
consequences (Fig. 2). Efforts aimed exclusively at suppress-
ing herbaceous vegetation had limited effectiveness in return-
ing structure to dry forest (cutting, herbicide, pulling, ID1, 2,
and 13; Table 1) but responses were more positive for rain for-
est (cutting, low-intensity grazing, ID8, 10, and 16), with the
exception of burning (ID12; Table 1). Promotion of propagule
supply without ﬁrst altering ground conditions had minimal
effect in the few cases where it was examined (ID2, 7, 8,
and 18; Table 1), except for one study where direct seeding
resulted in increased density of woody stems after 1.5 years
(ID10; Table 1). In general, there was an apparent trend for
interventions that combined manipulation of ground conditions
with actions to increase propagule supply to be most consistent
in promoting positive progress toward restoring forest struc-
ture (ID1, 2, 8, and 10; Table 1). This general pattern remains
evident even after accounting for the potential confounding
inﬂuence of the duration of intervention (Fig. 3).

label: Combined interventions vsalone
quote:
Two main interventions have been employed to increase
propagule supply: direct seeding and artiﬁcial bird perches.
However, these interventions have met with mixed success
in terms of promoting the return of forest structure. A
combination of interventions to increase propagule supply and
to suppress herbaceous vegetation has been more effective
than either intervention used alone (Holl et al. 2000; Posada
et al. 2000; Brooks et al. 2009; Ammondt et al. 2013),
consistent with the notion that tropical forest trees can be
both dispersal and establishment limited (Holl 2012). This
ﬁnding implies that multiple types of barriers to succession
likely need to be simultaneously overcome to achieve tangible
restoration progress (Reid & Holl 2013). It is surprising
then that combined interventions have not been tested more
frequently or implemented on larger spatial scales.
reason: Mechanistically explicit seedarrival pluscompetition removal but outcome simply return of foreststructure, heterogeneous variables. No homogeneous named VONT result; uncalibrated effect hold, not formal pooledmeta result.

label: Economic evidence
quote:
Finally, costs were reported in only 4 of 20 studies
that were quantitatively analyzed (Table S2), only 1 of
which made a comparison with the cost of tree planting
(Sampaio et al. 2007; but see also Cole et al. 2011; Kuaraksa
& Elliott 2012). There is clearly a need for more cost
accounting to better inform choices of intervention approach
to meet particular restoration goals. Such decisions may
involve complex trade-offs. For example, it is likely that
the initial cost of the low-intensity interventions considered
here would be less than for planting of nursery raised tree
seedlings (see also Rodrigues et al. 2009). However, this
lower establishment cost may be offset by a need for more
prolonged secondary treatment interventions, just as a lower
initial cost of lower density tree planting is offset by a longer
and more expensive subsequent maintenance schedule than
for high density planting (Hunt 2008; Rodrigues et al. 2009).
These ongoing interventions are largely driven by the need
to suppress aggressively competitive herbaceous vegetation
in the absence of a closed tree canopy. In order to reduce
the risk of uncertain outcomes from restoration investments
and enable the choice of cost effective intervention strategies,
future restoration experiments need to be coupled with longer
term quantitative assessments of both outcomes and costs
across a range of interventions.
reason: Fourstudies reportcosts, onlyone comparative treeplanting; S2 absent. No monetary amounts/denominators in mainpaper. Initial cheaper/ongoing dearer hypothesis not measured financial or cost effect.

label: Practice summary
quote:
Implications for Practice
• A wide range of intervention strategies, other than
tree planting, has emerged in the past two decades
to stimulate regeneration of tropical forest in disused
agricultural land.
• However, their outcomes and costs vary greatly, and
current knowledge is insufﬁcient to enable evidence
based choices of cost effective restoration method to suit
any particular restoration goal or circumstance. Further
carefully designed restoration experiments, coupled with
longer term quantitative assessments of costs and out-
comes, are needed to ﬁll these knowledge gaps.
• On the basis of the currently available information,
interventions which suppress herbaceous vegetation (e.g.
pasture grasses) and interventions which improve the
supply of plant propagules appear to be slightly more
effective at accelerating forest regeneration if used in
combination, but are infrequently effective when either
is used alone.
